extracted.intended_audience: neuroscientists, psychologists, and researchers studying reward, affect, and pleasure
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesis and evaluation of neuroscientific evidence about brain mechanisms of pleasure, hedonic 'liking' vs motivational 'wanting', and the roles of cortical and subcortical structures. Emphasizes methods and criteria for attributing pleasure generation to specific brain sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbitofrontal cortex as nexus for sensory integration and hedonic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The human orbitofrontal cortex is best thought of as an important nexus for sensory integration, emotional processing, and hedonic experience (Kringelbach 2004; Kringelbach 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: sensory identity decoded in primary sensory cortices -> posterior OFC for multimodal integration -> anterior OFC assigns reward value which can influence behavior (lateral anterior OFC), learning/memory (medial anterior OFC), and subjective hedonic experience (mid-anterior OFC). Medial OFC activity tends to correlate with positive valence, lateral OFC with unpleasant/avoidance-related stimuli, and mid-anterior OFC with state-dependent hedonic modulation (e.g., by satiety). Evidence comes from neuroimaging, neuropsychology, and neurophysiology; consider reciprocal connectivity with insula, ACC, nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, and amygdala. Useful for evaluating claims that OFC codes pleasure and for locating candidate regions for subjective experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate coding of affective valence versus sensation intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Affective valence of pleasure may be coded separately from sensation intensity in distinct brain regions (e.g., anterior insula codes taste intensity while medial orbitofrontal cortex codes subjective pleasantness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neuroimaging findings (de Araujo et al. 2003c) show that primary gustatory/insula activity tracks intensity but not valence, whereas medial OFC and anterior cingulate correlate with pleasantness ratings. Use this dissociation when interpreting imaging/behavioral data to avoid conflating intensity with hedonic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory-specific (selective) satiety to demonstrate reward-value coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective or sensory-specific satiety is a reinforcer-devaluation manipulation used to demonstrate coding of a stimulus's reward value by showing that satiety on one food selectively decreases its reward value and corresponding neural activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In neuroimaging, present two food stimuli before and after eating one to satiety; an area that tracks reward value should show decreased activity for the eaten food but not the other (Kringelbach et al. 2003; O'Doherty et al. 2000). Correlate neural changes with pleasantness ratings. This manipulation provides within-subject evidence that a region codes dynamic reward value rather than static sensory features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require necessity/sufficiency evidence before asserting cortical causation of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation of cortical activity with reported pleasure is insufficient to claim cortex causes subjective pleasure; one should test whether cortical sites are necessary or sufficient for normal pleasure reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal claims need lesion, stimulation, or other manipulations showing loss (necessity) or induction (sufficiency) of pleasurable states. Historical lobotomy and focal lesion data suggest basic 'liking' reactions can remain intact despite prefrontal damage, so interpret correlational neuroimaging cautiously. Proposed tests include focal lesions, precise stimulation, and measures of behavioral and subjective hedonic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hedonic 'liking' from motivational 'wanting' (incentive salience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate true hedonic impact ('liking') from incentive-salience-driven motivation or desire ('wanting'); they can be dissociated by brain manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize and measure 'liking' (e.g., orofacial reactions, subjective pleasantness ratings) separately from 'wanting' (e.g., effortful seeking, self-stimulation). Beware of interpreting increased pursuit/self-stimulation as increased pleasure; examples (dopamine manipulations, electrodes) often increase 'wanting' without boosting 'liking' (Berridge & Robinson 1998; Berridge 2003b). This distinction is central for interpreting pharmacological, stimulation, and lesion data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate mesolimbic dopamine roles beyond hedonic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Mesolimbic dopamine is often better characterized as coding predictive, motivational, or attentional properties of rewards (learning, prediction, incentive salience) rather than directly causing hedonic 'liking'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple evidence lines: dopamine neurons respond to predictive/attentional cues and sometimes to aversive stimuli; manipulations of dopamine often fail to shift 'liking' reliably; phasic vs tonic signaling distinctions matter for learning models. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations show that learning and cue-triggered performance can occur without canonical dopamine signals, complicating simple pleasure interpretations. Use caution before labeling dopamine as a pleasure neurotransmitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of brain stimulation/pleasure electrodes requires caution—self-stimulation may reflect 'wanting' not 'liking'
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic and modern cases of intracranial self-stimulation and DBS that produce vigorous self-stimulation or compulsive activation may not produce clear sensory pleasure, and may instead enhance motivation or incentive salience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case reports (e.g., Heath's B-19, Portenoy et al. 1986) show strong desire to stimulate without reports of clear pleasure expressions (no exclamations of 'that feels nice' or orgasms). Behavioral signs (compulsive button-pressing, neglect of hygiene) indicate enhanced wanting. Thus, do not equate high self-stimulation rates with hedonic pleasure; combine subjective reports, objective orofacial measures, and alternative assays to dissociate liking vs wanting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ convergent methods (neuroimaging, neuropsychology, neurophysiology, MEG, direct stimulation) to build stronger inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Converging evidence from multiple methodologies strengthens claims about which brain regions code or generate pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neuroimaging yields correlational maps; lesion studies test necessity; direct stimulation/DBS and MEG can probe causation and timing; single-unit physiology can reveal coding properties. Integrate across methods to distinguish coding, causation, and functional roles (e.g., OFC correlations plus lesion/stimulation tests). A single method is insufficient for strong causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider subcortical generators and evidence from cases with cortical atrophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of profound cortical loss (e.g., hydrocephalic children lacking much neocortex) who nevertheless express smiling and laughter suggest subcortical structures can generate basic affective reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These observations motivate alternative hypotheses that subcortex may be chief generator of basic 'liking' reactions; use such clinical and developmental cases to test cortex-versus-subcortex accounts. However, integrate with other data showing cortex's role in linking affect to complex cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret clinical anhedonia carefully: preserved sensory pleasure versus undervaluation in cognitive appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical anhedonia (depression, schizophrenia) may not reflect a total loss of sensory pleasure but instead an undervaluation of rewards in cognitive appraisal or life satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: many anhedonic patients still give essentially normal hedonic ratings to sucrose, suggesting intact basic 'liking' with possible impairments in higher-order valuation, anticipation, or decision processes. When assessing anhedonia, measure both immediate sensory 'liking' and cognitive evaluations/anticipatory pleasure to distinguish mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and localize hedonic 'hotspots' distinct from motivational substrates
rubrics_metrics.description: True brain hedonic hotspots (e.g., opioid-related hotspots) are distinguished by their ability to generate or amplify 'liking' reactions, unlike broader motivational systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify hotspots via manipulations that increase objective hedonic reactions (e.g., taste reactivity) and subjective pleasantness, not merely increased consumption or seeking. Contrast with mesolimbic dopamine and stimulation sites that often enhance 'wanting' without enhancing hedonic impact. Localize hotspots (e.g., ventral pallidum, nucleus accumbens shell microdomains) and test causally.
